extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and practitioners (especially biotech/pharmaceutical applicants) and those filing at the EPO/PCT
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on the formal requirements for patent drawings under the PCT and EPC, with emphasis on how those rules apply (or fail to apply) to scientific data and photographs used to support biotech/pharma patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of patent drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings function to aid understanding of an invention and contribute to correct disclosure of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embodiments of mechanical inventions may be easier to explain as drawings than by lengthy description; scientific data are intended to demonstrate plausibility or support claims but may not serve the same purpose or naturally conform to technical-illustration style requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation for direct reproduction (Rule 11(a) PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings, like all other parts of the application, must be 'presented as to admit of direct reproduction by photography, electrostatic processes, photo offset, and microfilming, in any number of copies' (Rule 11(a) PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a functional requirement about reproducibility/formatting rather than content; it underpins many of the form rules (size, darkness, line quality) that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black line / no colouring requirement (Rule 11(a) PCT / Rule 46 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings shall be executed in durable, black, sufficiently dense and dark, uniformly thick and well-defined, lines and strokes without colorings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement makes sense for technical illustrations of mechanical objects but can be ill-suited to scientific data (e.g., bar charts, gels, immuno‑fluorescence) that rely on colour or shading to convey information; compliance often forces use of cross-hatching or other workarounds that reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special drawing provisions (Rule 11.3(a)-(n) PCT and Rule 46 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are enumerated, special requirements governing the form of drawings in the PCT and EPC (Rule 11.3(a)-(n) PCT; Rule 46 EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These detailed provisions were drafted with mechanical illustrations in mind; their precise content (margins, reference signs, scales, numbering, line types, etc.) can be burdensome or inappropriate when applied to graphs, charts, photographs or other scientific figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow sheets and diagrams deemed drawings (Rule 46(3) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPC (but not the PCT) stipulates that 'flow sheets and diagrams shall be deemed to be drawings' (Rule 46(3) EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit recognition that non‑mechanical schematic figures can be treated as drawings under the EPC, but it does not fully address other scientific data forms (e.g., charts, gel images).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs and scales treated restrictively (Rule 11(f) PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11(f) PCT states that a scale (even a graphical one) should only be drawn in 'exceptional' cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT thus disfavors inclusion of graphical scales and, by extension, may be hostile to graphs/charts essential for communicating scientific data, increasing friction for biotech/pharma disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO allowance for shading (EPO Guidelines A‑IX 7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO Guidelines for Examination indicate that 'the use of shading in figures is allowed provided this assists in their understanding and is not so extensive to impede legibility' (A‑IX 7.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO practice is more flexible than the literal black‑lines rule; limited shading may be acceptable where it helps comprehension. This is a practical concession for certain scientific or schematic figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs allowed only where necessary; PCT black‑and‑white rule (PCT applicant's guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT makes no provision for photographs but allows them where it is impossible to present in a drawing what is to be shown; 'Where, exceptionally, photographs are submitted, they must be black and white...Color photographs are not accepted, nor are color drawings' (PCT applicant's guide, 5.159).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs (e.g., Western blots, immuno‑fluorescence, organism photos) are permitted only in exceptional cases and must be B/W under PCT practice, which can limit their utility for scientific evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO practice on colour photographs (EPO Guidelines A‑IX 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO Guidelines indicate that photographs may be permitted 'where it is impossible to present in a drawing what is to be shown…Colour photographs are accepted, but will be scanned, printed and made available via file inspection only in black and white' (A‑IX 1.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the EPO may accept colour photos, they will be rendered B/W in the public/printed record; this reduces value of colour-coded data and creates inconsistency between submission and inspection versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving Section discretion and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the EPC lacks a specific provision for many types of scientific figures, the extent to which scientific data must conform to Rule 46 EPC can be open to the discretion of the EPO Receiving Section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates uncertainty for applicants: different receiving/examination staff may take different views on whether data figures comply, leading to inconsistent requirements and potential additional work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction and refusal procedure for defective drawings (Rule 48 EPC and Article 90(5) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the EPO finds drawings do not satisfy Rule 46 EPC, they issue an invitation to remedy the deficiencies within two months (Rule 48 EPC); failure to remedy properly or on time can lead to refusal of the application (Article 90(5) EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑compliance has concrete procedural consequences; applicants must remedy drawing defects promptly to avoid refusal, which can impose time and cost burdens when scientific data are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical anti‑pattern: forcing scientific data into black‑and‑white technical drawing format
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting scientific figures (bar charts, gels, immuno‑fluorescence images) into black‑and‑white cross‑hatched, text‑free drawings to comply with formal requirements often reduces clarity and communication of the underlying data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conversions can be time‑consuming and expensive and may result in figures that are worse at communicating the data than the originals; this argues for reconsideration of whether scientific data should be treated under the same drawing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology and categorization concern — consider separate category for scientific data
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'drawings' is inappropriate for many types of graphical illustration (software, biotech, pharmaceutical data); data might be better submitted under a different category akin to supplementary data of a scientific article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests rethinking the rigid application of drawing formalities to data and proposes treating scientific figures differently to preserve their communicative value while satisfying reproducibility/file formatting needs.
